title: Database Production Operations: Backups, Migrations, and Monitoring
learningObjectives: Distinguish a backup from a proven recovery process.
Explain RPO, RTO, WAL, and point-in-time recovery.
Diagnose pool saturation, lock waits, query regressions, and storage growth.
Measure index size and observed usage, distinguish size from bloat, and assess dependencies before replacing or removing an index.

mentalModel.text: Production database work means proving the system can change, fail, and recover without losing more data or availability than the business accepts. A backup is useful only if it can be restored, a migration is safe only if old and new application versions can coexist, and monitoring is useful only when it helps find the bottleneck.

concepts.title: Backups, restore drills, RPO, and RTO

blocks.text: A backup job proves a copy was created; a restore drill proves the copy can recover a usable database. Recovery planning starts with two business targets.

blocks.title: Recovery terms
rows: Five minutes means at most about five minutes of recent data loss.
Thirty minutes means recovery should finish within thirty minutes.

blocks.problem: A team has nightly backups but has never restored one. A backup from 02:00 may be too old or unusable if production fails at 21:00.
reasoning: Choose RPO/RTO from business impact, not the current schedule.
Restore to an isolated environment and verify integrity, credentials, keys, and application queries.
Keep recovery copies separate from the primary failure domain.
blocks.outcome: A recovery plan needs tested backups, measured restore time, and an explicit acceptable data-loss window.

blocks.text: A base backup captures a starting state. PostgreSQL write-ahead log (WAL) records changes that can be replayed after that point. With the required base backup and continuous WAL archive, point-in-time recovery can restore to a time before an accidental change.

blocks.source:
Base backup + archived WAL
→ restore base backup
→ replay WAL to target time
→ validate recovered database
blocks.title: PITR sequence
WAL is not a backup by itself
blocks.content: WAL alone does not replace a base backup and tested restore procedure. Archive gaps, retention, encryption keys, and configuration affect whether recovery is possible.

blocks.problem: A table is accidentally deleted at 14:05. Restore to an isolated target just before 14:05, replay available WAL, verify the table, then follow an approved cutover procedure.
reasoning: Do not overwrite production during investigation; restore separately first.
The target time must fall within available backup and WAL coverage.
Measure validation and cutover time, not only replay time.
blocks.outcome: PITR is a tested sequence of backup, WAL retention, restore, replay, validation, and controlled cutover.

blocks.text: A rolling deployment can run old and new application versions at once. Dropping or renaming a column immediately can break old instances still using it.

blocks.title: Phase
rows: Add the new nullable column or compatible structure.
Deploy code that understands old and new shapes.
Copy old values in bounded, restartable batches.
Use the new shape after validation.
Remove the old field only after every old consumer is gone.

blocks.problem: To split full_name into first_name and last_name, add the new columns, deploy compatible code, backfill in batches, verify, switch reads, and remove the old column in a later release.
reasoning: Backfills should be restartable and idempotent.
Large updates can create WAL, locks, and replica lag; monitor production impact.
Application rollback does not automatically undo a destructive data migration.
blocks.outcome: Use expand-and-contract so schema and application changes do not require every instance to switch simultaneously.

blocks.text: A schema migration can be logically correct and still create too much downtime if it scans a large live table under a strong lock. For PostgreSQL, one way to enforce uniqueness with less write blocking is to clean up duplicates, prevent new duplicates during the rollout, create a unique index concurrently, verify the index is valid, then attach it as a constraint. Plan the exact sequence for the PostgreSQL version and table type.

blocks.title: Build and verify a concurrent unique index

blocks.text: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` must be run outside an explicit transaction block. It uses more work and may take longer; monitor its progress, lock waits, write latency, and replication lag. If it fails, inspect the catalog flags and server logs before retrying. An invalid concurrent unique index can still enforce uniqueness in some failure states, so do not assume every invalid index is harmless. The exact recovery step depends on the failed phase and index type.

concepts.title: Index operations: measure, replace, and remove safely

blocks.text: Indexes are production objects: they consume disk, use cache space when their pages are hot, and add work to writes. An index change should start with the real query it supports and a baseline—not with the assumption that a bigger or more-used index is always better.

blocks.title: Measure index size and observed usage
blocks.source:
SELECT s.schemaname,
       s.relname AS table_name,
       s.indexrelname AS index_name,
       s.idx_scan, s.idx_tup_read, s.idx_tup_fetch,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid)) AS index_size
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes AS s
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(s.indexrelid) DESC;

blocks.text: Index size and index bloat are not the same thing. `pg_relation_size` reports the space occupied by the index; it does not estimate how much is wasted. The `pg_stat_user_indexes` counters describe the observed workload since statistics were last reset, so inspect `stats_reset` and measure a representative period before deciding an index is unused.

blocks.title: Optional B-tree page inspection with pgstattuple
What to check before an index change
rows: Is the index large or growing?
Size trend and table/index growth rate
Large size alone does not prove bloat.
Representative query workload, index definition, predicates, sort order, included columns, operator class, and constraint dependencies
A zero scan count in a short window is not proof an index is safe to drop.
Table size, free disk, write load, build progress, locks, and replica lag
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY reduces write blocking but takes more work and has restrictions.
Dependency/constraint check, rollback plan, and evidence the replacement serves the workload
A primary/unique constraint may depend on an index; removing it can change correctness, not just speed.

steps.title: 1. Capture a baseline
steps.description: Record the slow query, EXPLAIN plan, p95/p99 latency, index size, and write overhead over a representative workload window.

steps.title: 2. Build the candidate carefully
steps.description: For a large live table, consider CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY when its restrictions fit. Run it outside an explicit transaction block and monitor disk space, I/O, locks, errors, and replica lag.

steps.title: 3. Validate the result
steps.description: Check that the index is valid, compare query plans and observed latency, and verify uniqueness or other constraints where applicable.

steps.title: 4. Retire the old index only with evidence
steps.description: Check constraint ownership and dependencies, confirm the workload no longer needs the old definition, and prefer DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY where appropriate and supported.

steps.title: 5. Observe after rollout
steps.description: Monitor query latency, errors, write throughput, disk usage, and replica lag. Keep a clear recovery plan if the new index performs worse.

blocks.problem: A 300 GB orders table is gaining a new status/created_at index, and the team also suspects an older index is redundant.
reasoning: Capture the affected query plan and representative latency first. Inspect the candidate index size and available disk before starting.
Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY if appropriate for the live workload; monitor its progress and expect additional I/O and CPU. If it fails, inspect catalog state and logs before retrying.
Compare both index definitions and query patterns. A similar leading column is not enough: sort order, predicates, included columns, operator classes, uniqueness, and constraints may differ.
Only remove the old index after the candidate is valid and measurements show it serves the workload. Use concurrent drop where appropriate and avoid dropping constraint-owned indexes directly.
blocks.outcome: Safe index operations prove the benefit, preserve availability, and include a checked failure path—not merely a CREATE or DROP command.

blocks.text: Connections consume resources. Too many concurrent queries can increase memory use, lock contention, and tail latency. A pool limits concurrency; timeouts and backpressure stop queues from growing without bound.

blocks.title: Symptom
rows: Lock graph, pool waits, wait events
EXPLAIN ANALYZE, BUFFERS, estimates vs actual rows

blocks.problem: A service opens 500 connections although the database handles about 40 active queries efficiently. Increasing the pool may move the queue into the database and worsen latency.
reasoning: Size pools from measured database capacity and query duration, not web-request count alone.
Use connection/statement timeouts and bounded queues.
Retries should be bounded with backoff; retry storms can amplify overload.
blocks.outcome: Diagnose the wait or expensive plan node before tuning; monitor pool waits and p95/p99 latency together.

blocks.text: 1. Problem and motivation — A deployment removes a column while old application instances still use it, causing production errors.
2. Definition and design choice — Expand-and-contract adds the new shape first, keeps code compatible, backfills and verifies data, switches reads, then removes the old shape later.

blocks.problem: The old application reads full_name; the new app reads first_name and last_name.
reasoning: Add new columns without removing full_name, then deploy code that supports both forms.
Backfill in bounded, restartable batches and monitor WAL, locks, and replica lag.
Switch reads after verification, then remove the old column after all old consumers are gone.
blocks.outcome: Compatibility across rollout stages avoids requiring every application instance to change at the same instant.

blocks.text: 4. Trade-offs and scale — Bounded batches reduce lock and WAL pressure but take longer. Aggressive migrations can shorten the window but raise production risk.
5. Anti-patterns — Dropping the old column in the first deploy, one giant backfill at peak traffic, and assuming code rollback reverses a data migration.
6. Interview probes — What if backfill stops halfway? How do old and new versions coexist? How would you recover an accidental delete? What do RPO and RTO measure?

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: A green backup job is not proof of recoverability
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content: Recovery depends on backup integrity, WAL coverage, permissions, keys, configuration, restore time, and application-level validation.

revisionSheet.text: RPO = acceptable data-loss window. RTO = acceptable time to restore service.
PITR needs a base backup plus the required WAL history and a tested restore procedure.
Expand-and-contract: expand schema → compatible code → backfill → switch reads → contract later.
Pool limits, timeouts, backpressure, and bounded retries protect the database from overload.
Diagnose from metrics, waits, plans, and recent changes; do not tune blindly.

options.text: Target time to restore service
Acceptable data-loss window
Number of indexes

questions.explanation: RPO describes how much recent data loss is acceptable.

options.text: Target time to restore service
Acceptable data-loss window
Sort duration

questions.explanation: RTO describes the target duration to restore service.

questions.prompt: What does WAL do in a PITR workflow?

options.text: Replay changes after a base backup to a target time
Replace every base backup
Guarantee no data loss ever

questions.explanation: PITR combines a base backup with the required WAL history.

questions.prompt: Why can increasing a connection pool worsen latency?

options.text: It makes SQL invalid
It can overload the database with concurrent work
It disables indexes

questions.explanation: Too much concurrency can increase contention rather than throughput.

questions.prompt: Large backfills should be planned for WAL, locks, replication lag, restartability, and production load.
questions.explanation: Backfills affect storage, replicas, locks, and latency; bounded batches and monitoring reduce risk.

questions.prompt: What does PostgreSQL point-in-time recovery normally require?

options.text: A base backup and the needed continuous WAL archive to replay to the target time
Only a read replica
Only the latest schema dump
An index on every timestamp column

questions.explanation: PITR restores a base backup and replays archived WAL up to the chosen point, provided the required chain is available.

questions.prompt: Why keep the old column during the first deploy of an expand-and-contract migration?

options.text: Old application instances may still be reading or writing it while old and new versions coexist
PostgreSQL cannot add new columns
Columns cannot be dropped in PostgreSQL
The new application cannot use SQL

questions.explanation: A rolling deployment can run application versions at once. Removing the old shape before every consumer is migrated can break older instances.

questions.prompt: A concurrent index build fails and leaves an invalid index. What is the safest next step?

options.text: Inspect its catalog state, server logs, dependencies, and failure phase before deciding whether to drop/rebuild
Assume it has no write overhead and ignore it forever
Immediately rerun CREATE INDEX with the same name without checking
Drop the table

questions.explanation: An invalid index may consume storage/write overhead, and a failed unique concurrent build can have special enforcement behavior. Investigate first.

questions.prompt: A database allows 120 client connections. Three services each configure pools of 50, before migrations and admin sessions. What is the main problem?

options.text: Their combined possible demand (150) already exceeds the whole server budget, leaving no headroom for other clients
Each service will automatically share one pool
Connection count does not affect resource use
Set every pool to 120

questions.explanation: Plan a global connection budget across replicas/services, reserve operational headroom, and cap concurrency. More connections can increase contention.

questions.prompt: API p95 jumps from 100 ms to 1.4 seconds, while pool wait time rises and the database shows many active sessions. What should you do first?

options.text: Increase every pool and retry without limits
Measure pool wait, active/idle-in-transaction sessions, lock waits, and query plans; then reduce or queue concurrency at the actual bottleneck
Drop indexes
Disable statement timeouts

questions.explanation: Break the latency into queueing, query execution, locks, I/O, and application time. Increasing concurrency without evidence can worsen saturation.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL index occupies 20 GB on disk. What does that number tell you by itself?

options.text: The index has exactly 20 GB of wasted space
Its current on-disk size is 20 GB, but more evidence is needed to estimate bloat
It uses 20 GB of RAM at all times

questions.explanation: pg_relation_size measures index file size, not wasted space. Use trends and, when appropriate, detailed B-tree inspection such as pgstatindex from pgstattuple.

questions.prompt: An index has `idx_scan = 0` during a one-hour monitoring window. What is the safest next step?

options.text: Drop it immediately because the statistic proves it is useless
Check a representative workload period and verify constraints and dependencies before considering removal
Reboot the database

questions.explanation: Statistics can reset and rare jobs may use the index. Some indexes are needed for uniqueness or constraints even when scan counts are low.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A team has nightly backups but needs an RPO of five minutes and an RTO of thirty minutes. What should you test?
strongAnswerPoints: Nightly backups alone likely do not meet a five-minute RPO.
Evaluate WAL archiving or another recovery mechanism.
Restore to an isolated target and measure replay, validation, and cutover.
Verify permissions, keys, integrity, and failure-domain separation.
pitfalls: Assuming nightly backups meet a five-minute RPO
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: Nightly backups alone likely cannot meet a five-minute data-loss window. I would evaluate continuous WAL archiving, then perform restore drills and measure replay, validation, and cutover against the thirty-minute RTO. The runbook must include keys, permissions, integrity checks, and a safe target.

interviewScenarios.prompt: Split full_name into first_name and last_name while the application stays online. Outline a safe migration.
strongAnswerPoints: Add new columns without dropping the old field.
Deploy code compatible with both shapes.
Backfill in bounded batches and verify completeness.
Switch reads, then drop the old field in a later release.
pitfalls: Dropping the old column before old instances are gone
One giant update without measuring WAL or locks
Assuming code rollback undoes data migration
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: Use expand-and-contract: add the new columns, deploy code compatible with both shapes, backfill in bounded batches, verify values, switch reads, and remove the old column only after all old instances and consumers are gone. Monitor locks, WAL, replica lag, and errors.
